Chapter 1: The Unspoken Standard — Discovering the Moral Law
Have you ever found yourself in a quiet argument? Maybe it’s over a borrowed book that was never returned, a promise someone broke, or just a careless word that stung a little too much.
Think about that moment—two friends, voices getting louder, each one sure they’re right. One says, “That’s not fair!” and the other fires back, “But you promised!” What’s really going on here?
Underneath all that, there’s something deeper at play. Both people are appealing to a kind of invisible rulebook, as if everyone’s supposed to know the rules about what’s right and what’s wrong.
What’s fascinating is, nobody really teaches this sense of fairness the way we learn math or grammar. It’s not something you memorize in school, and it’s definitely not just a matter of personal taste. Even little kids, before they can even explain it, somehow know when things aren’t right.
Sure, they might not always stick to the rules themselves, but they sure expect everyone else to do it. This feeling is so common, we barely notice it—kind of like the air we breathe.
Now, here’s something interesting. When someone gets caught breaking this unwritten code, their first instinct usually isn’t to deny the rule exists. Instead, they try to excuse what they did—maybe with, “I had no choice,” or “You started it.”
That tells us a lot. Deep down, people believe there’s a real standard out there, and they expect it to apply to everyone—including themselves.
Some folks will say this sense of right and wrong just comes from culture or the way we’re raised. But when you look across different countries and different times in history, the basic ideas don’t really change. Customs might look different, but honesty, fairness, keeping promises—these show up everywhere.
And if someone suggested that betrayal or cruelty are good things? Most of us would feel a gut-level reaction and pull away.
Others say this moral sense is just about convenience—a way to help people get along. But that doesn’t quite capture it. The feeling of obligation goes much deeper. It’s not just about what works best; it’s about what really should be done, even if it’s hard or uncomfortable.
There’s a big difference between saying, “I want to,” and, “I should.” You can feel that difference, can’t you? It’s not just in your head—it’s in your gut.
Here’s the tension: We all know the standard, but we don’t always live up to it. The gap between what’s expected and what we actually do can lead to frustration, guilt, even shame.
It’s easy to notice where others fall short, but it’s much tougher to admit it in ourselves. Still, the standard is always there—unyielding, constant.
So what does all this point to? This universal sense of right and wrong suggests there’s something bigger than personal opinions or group traditions. It hints at a real, objective moral law—a law that stands above what any one person or society might want.
And if there’s a law like that, you can’t help but wonder… where does it come from?
The idea of a moral lawgiver starts to take shape—not just as some abstract theory, but as a living question that’s woven into our everyday lives.
